# 2026 Annual Budget Review

## Summary
I did this year's review on the last Sunday of December, with the statements exported to a single sheet and a mug of tea going cold beside me. The savings rate came out at 31% of take-home pay, the best figure I have recorded and a real step up from the year before. Some of that is the pay rise I got in April, some of it is the rent coming down after I renegotiated the renewal, and a good slice is simply the habits being boring by now. Income was steady across the twelve months apart from that rise, and I did not take on any second work. I kept paying myself first, though I moved the transfer to the day after payday rather than waiting for the first working day, which lands the money out of reach a little sooner. There was one large purchase, a laptop, which I had planned and paid for from savings rather than credit. The year needed no drama to produce the number, and that is the part I am quietly pleased about.

The interesting shift this year was that the fixed costs finally became the smaller half of the picture. For years rent and utilities ate most of the take-home before anything else could be considered, and the only real lever was groceries and the odd treat. This year the balance tipped, and the surplus started doing some of the work itself. That is the change I want to protect, because it is the one that compounds.

## Expenses
Rent held at 30% of income after I renegotiated the renewal, which is the first time it has not crept upward in four years. The landlord wanted a longer term and I traded that for a flat figure, and it has already paid for itself. Groceries averaged 430 EUR a month, up a little on last year partly through higher prices at the till and partly through eating better, with more fresh fish and less of the cheap filler. The heating direct debit sat at 145 EUR a month, steady across the year, which was a relief after the volatility of the previous winters. Utilities and insurance both stayed close to plan. Transport came in lower than expected because I cycled through the warmer months and only drove when the weather turned. I bought a laptop for the work-from-home days, planned rather than impulsive, and paid for it outright. Subscriptions are trimmed to the few I actually use. The one overshoot was a short trip in the autumn, but it came out of the holiday pot I had built through the spring. Everything else behaved. The laptop drew the emergency cushion down by a chunk, which I have noted as the one thing to rebuild through next year. Car costs were light because the bike did the commuting for most of the warmer months. I also moved the phone contract to a cheaper plan in June, which saved a few euros a month and cost nothing but an afternoon on the phone. None of that changes the headline figure, but it is the kind of quiet saving that makes the rate possible without the year feeling tight.

## Next Year
For next year I want the surplus to work harder rather than sit in cash. The plan is 500 EUR a month into index funds, set as a standing order the day after payday so it happens without me thinking about it, the same trick that made paying myself first stick. That is the headline change and the rest is tidying. I will hold the rent at its current share if the renewal allows, keep groceries near the 430 EUR mark, and top the holiday pot a little more so the autumn trip does not feel tight. I also want to build the emergency cushion back to six months of costs, since the laptop purchase drew it down and I would rather not run that thin again. If the income rises, the extra goes to the investments first and the lifestyle second, and I will say that out loud now so the January version of me cannot forget it. If groceries run over, the difference comes out of the dining out line rather than the investments, which are the one thing I do not want to touch once they are set.
